app.title: Temperature Analyser v1.0
app.summary: The person registers a vertical well: its name, whether it is onshore or offshore, its kelly bushing and ground level or water depth, and the mean temperature at the surface or sea floor. Before drilling, they enter low, mid and high (P90, P50, P10) geothermal gradients and a total depth. The tool then predicts temperature every 500 m down the well and shows the result as a table and as depth–temperature curves. They can choose which depth reference to plot against. After drilling, they enter measured depth and bottom-hole temperature for up to six logging runs. Each run is corrected by two published methods, and the corrected temperatures and interval geothermal gradients are shown in a table and in two depth profiles. A separate tab converts between common length and temperature units.

task.text: Predict a well's temperature-with-depth profile from gradient scenarios before drilling, then correct measured bottom-hole temperatures and derive geothermal gradients after drilling.

data.text: A handful of numbers typed in for one well: reference levels, a surface temperature, gradient scenarios and paired depth–temperature readings from logging runs. These are turned into tables of depth against temperature and gradient.
data.item: a depth point in a vertical well, with a temperature or gradient at that depth

stage.text: planning a well's thermal conditions before drilling, and analysing logged bottom-hole temperatures after it

mechanism.text: The tabs run from well registration through pre-drill prediction to post-drill analysis. The registration values feed both calculation tabs, and the region choice sets the depth references offered. On each calculation tab, a form of numeric inputs and an input-check dialog lead to a Calculate button. The button fills a results table next to depth-reversed line charts, where each scenario or correction method is a coloured curve the person can recolour.

field.text: bottom-hole temperature correction and geothermal gradient prediction for exploration wells in petroleum geoscience

workflow.name: predict a profile from scenario parameters, then correct measurements against it

steps.step: describe the setting the calculation depends on
steps.here: Well registration tab: well name, onshore/offshore radio, kelly bushing level, ground level or water depth, and mean annual surface or sea-floor temperature, with an Input Check dialog that flags impossible reference levels

steps.step: enter scenario parameters and check they are consistent
steps.here: P90, P50 and P10 geothermal gradients (°C/km) and a total depth. The '?' check confirms that P90 < P50 < P10

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: Calculate & Display lists depths every 500 m down to total depth and predicts the temperature at each for the three gradients. Results show in a table and as three depth-reversed curves; a dropdown picks the depth reference and others pick each curve's colour
Measured depth and bottom-hole temperature (°F) are typed in for up to six logging runs. Input Check requires the depths to increase from run to run

steps.step: compute corrected values by more than one method and set them side by side
steps.here: Each run's depth is converted to true vertical depth, and its temperature is corrected with the AAPG polynomial and with Harrison et al. (1983), then converted to °C. Interval geothermal gradients are computed from the surface temperature down. Results go into a table and two overlaid depth profiles, one for temperature and one for gradient
Pick one of twelve length or temperature conversions, type a value, and read the result to two decimals

distinctive: Depths are worked out from measured depth using the kelly bushing and ground level or water depth. Onshore wells offer TVDkb/TVDgl and offshore wells TVDbml, and the region choice changes the depth options offered
Pre-drill prediction carries three probabilistic gradient scenarios (P90/P50/P10), which must be ordered P90 < P50 < P10
Logged bottom-hole temperatures are corrected by two published empirical methods (AAPG and Harrison et al. 1983), and their temperatures and gradients are overlaid on the same charts
Depth runs downward on the vertical axis of every chart, as in a well log
